title: Real images of real things
statement: Use a real image for any real place, object or document students may have to recognise, not a generated likeness.
detail: Review of generated articles asked why generated images stood in for real monuments that students will probably have to identify on the exam, since a generated image often doesn't resemble a photograph of the real thing (`icloud-work/k_12_social_studies/ap_files/Articles Tracker.xlsx`, sheet 'Articles-readable-exp', cell M12). Another note named a famous real image to use instead (sheet 'APUSH Articles', cell M38).
against: A real image raises rights questions: one note accepted the generated images in case the real one was under copyright (sheet 'APUSH Articles-readable-exp', cell M28: "If this is copyrighted, the ones you have work."), though the same cell records that a copyright-free real image was then added.

evidence.quote: When there are historical examples like Angkor Wat or Angkor Tom, why aren't we using actual images? Students will probably have to be able to identify these images on the exam, so why are we relying on AI generated images which often do not resemble fow the image would look in an existing photograph?
Some circulating crops actually show the Hope theatre
An accurate labelled schematic is preferable to a misidentified historical image.
Use a real historical depiction of textile work only if its period and provenance are correct. An original labelled role diagram is sufficient.
The U1 photograph candidate did not clearly establish entry geometry without additional work, so production uses an explicit schematic.
